title: Slavery in the Bible
lead: Israel's story begins with God freeing slaves from Egypt, yet its laws regulate slavery rather than abolish it, and the New Testament addresses slaves and masters. How to read these texts honestly was fought over in the abolition debates and still matters.

sections.b: Israel's laws regulate slavery in three main places. Exodus 21:2–11 frees the Hebrew slave after six years. Deuteronomy 15:12–18 extends the release to women and requires gifts on leaving, and Deuteronomy 23:15–16 forbids handing a runaway slave back. Leviticus 25:39–46 says an Israelite in debt must be treated as a hired worker until the Jubilee, but allows foreigners to be bought and held for life. Jeremiah 34:8–22 condemns Jerusalem for freeing slaves and taking them back, and Nehemiah 5:1–13 attacks debt slavery among Jews.
sections.refs: Exodus 21:2–11; Deuteronomy 15:12–18; Deuteronomy 23:15–16; Leviticus 25:39–46; Jeremiah 34:8–22; Nehemiah 5:1–13

sections.b: The New Testament household codes tell slaves to obey and masters to be fair, reminding both that they have one Master in heaven (Ephesians 6:5–9; Colossians 3:22–4:1; 1 Peter 2:18). Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon "no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave: a much-loved brother" (Philemon 16) and says that in Christ there is "no slave or free" (Galatians 3:28); 1 Timothy 1:10 condemns slave traders. In the Atlantic abolition debates both sides used these texts. Many Christians today see the gospel's logic as finally against slavery; critics answer that the Bible never forbids it outright.
sections.refs: Ephesians 6:5–9; Colossians 3:22–4:1; 1 Peter 2:18–25; Philemon 15–16; Galatians 3:28; 1 Timothy 1:10
